config.title: Write identity generic and explain inference

intro.title: Write identity generic and explain inference
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple but powerful function called `identity`. This function will take any input value and return that same value unchanged. You will learn how to write this function using TypeScript generics, which allow the function to work with many different data types while keeping full type safety. The core concept is type inference, where TypeScript automatically figures out the correct type based on the argument you pass. By the end, you'll understand how to declare a generic function and how TypeScript infers types to make your code both flexible and robust.
intro.usecase: Generic functions like identity are foundational in TypeScript applications where data needs to be processed without losing type information. In a dashboard component, you might use identity to pass user data through validation pipelines while preserving the exact User type. When building a form library, identity functions help transform input values while maintaining strict typing for autocomplete and error checking. This pattern appears in API response handlers where you need to return the same data structure that was received, ensuring type safety throughout your application.

objectives: Implement a generic identity function that accepts and returns any type
Apply type parameters to create reusable type-safe functions
Construct a generic function with explicit type arguments
Configure TypeScript to infer types automatically from function arguments
Manipulate generic constraints to control acceptable type parameters
Initialize a generic function with different primitive and object types
Integrate type inference with generic functions in practical scenarios

steps.title: Import TypeScript types and utilities
steps.instruction: Import the TypeScript types and utilities that will be used throughout this lesson. Add the import statement at the top of the file.
steps.hint: You'll need to import from TypeScript's built-in utilities. Start with 'import' followed by what you need from 'typescript'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing a utility
import { UtilityName } from 'typescript';
steps.seedCode: // Import the necessary TypeScript types and utilities here
steps.expectedOutcome: The file will have the proper imports for TypeScript's type system utilities.
successCriteria: TypeScript types and utilities are imported from 'typescript'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you're importing from 'typescript' and including the necessary utilities.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to import TypeScript types and utilities from the 'typescript' module.

steps.title: Create a basic identity function without generics
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'identity' that takes one parameter called 'value' of type 'any' and returns that same value.
steps.hint: Start with 'function identity(value: any): any { }' or use an arrow function. Inside the function body, simply return the 'value' parameter.
steps.seedCode:
// Import the necessary TypeScript types and utilities here

// Create your identity function here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a working identity function that accepts any type of value and returns it, but it lacks type safety.
successCriteria: The identity function is defined with a parameter 'value' typed as 'any' and returns the same value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function takes a parameter of type 'any' and returns it. Check the function name and return statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match the requirement. You need to create a function named 'identity' that takes a value of type 'any' and returns it.

steps.title: Add type parameter to create a generic identity function
steps.instruction: Convert your existing identity function to use a generic type parameter 'T' instead of 'any' in the parameter and return type.
steps.hint: Replace 'any' with a type parameter like <T> before the parameter list, then use T for the parameter type and return type.
steps.expectedOutcome: The identity function should now have a generic type parameter T, making it type-safe while preserving the ability to work with any type.
successCriteria: The identity function uses a generic type parameter T instead of any for both parameter and return type.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to use the generic type parameter T for both the parameter type and return type instead of any.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function still uses 'any' types. Try adding a type parameter <T> before the parameter list and use T for both the parameter and return type.

steps.title: Test the generic identity function with explicit type arguments
steps.instruction: Call your identity function twice: once with an explicit type argument of <string> and the value 'Hello', and once with <number> and the value 42. Log both results to the console.
steps.hint: Use the syntax identity<string>('Hello') to call the function with an explicit type argument. Then call identity<number>(42).
steps.expectedOutcome: The console will log 'Hello' and 42, showing that the generic function works with different types when explicit type arguments are provided.
successCriteria: The identity function is called twice with explicit type arguments <string> and <number>, and both results are logged to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling identity with explicit type arguments (e.g., identity<string>('Hello')) and logging both results to the console.
steps.feedbackWrong: call the identity function twice with explicit type arguments: once for string and once for number, then log both results.

steps.title: Demonstrate TypeScript's type inference with generics
steps.instruction: Call your identity function without providing explicit type arguments, letting TypeScript infer the type from the argument you pass.
steps.hint: Simply call identity() with a value of any type (like a string or number) and assign the result to a variable. Don't write <Type> before the argument.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: function call with inferred type
const inferredResult = identity('hello'); // TypeScript infers T as string
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll see that TypeScript automatically infers the generic type parameter T based on the argument you pass, without needing to specify it explicitly.
successCriteria: The identity function is called without explicit type arguments, and the result is stored in a variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You called the function, but make sure you didn't provide explicit type arguments (like identity<string>('hello')). Try calling it as identity('hello') instead.
steps.feedbackWrong: The identity function wasn't called without explicit type arguments. Review the instruction: call identity(value) and let TypeScript infer T.

steps.title: Create a generic function with multiple type parameters
steps.instruction: Create a new function named 'pair' that takes two generic type parameters T and U, accepts two arguments of those types, and returns them as a tuple.
steps.hint: Define the function with two type parameters in angle brackets: function pair<T, U>(first: T, second: U). Return an array containing both arguments.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new generic function 'pair' with two type parameters that returns a tuple of its two arguments.
successCriteria: The 'pair' function is defined with two generic type parameters T and U, takes two arguments of those types, and returns a tuple [T, U].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function has two type parameters (T and U), accepts two arguments with those types, and returns them as a tuple [first, second].
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't quite right. You need to create a function named 'pair' that uses two generic type parameters and returns a tuple containing both arguments.

steps.title: Test type inference with multiple generic parameters
steps.instruction: Call the pair function with two different argument types, letting TypeScript infer both type parameters.
steps.hint: Invoke the pair function with two arguments of different types, like a string and a number, without specifying the type parameters explicitly.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should see that TypeScript correctly infers both type parameters from the arguments you pass.
successCriteria: The pair function is called with two arguments of different types, and no explicit type arguments are provided.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling the pair function with two different argument types and letting TypeScript infer the types.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're calling the pair function with two arguments and allowing TypeScript to infer the types automatically.

steps.title: Add constraints to generic type parameters
steps.instruction: Create a new generic function named 'getLength' with a type parameter constrained to types that have a 'length' property. The function should take a value of that type and return its length.
steps.hint: Use the 'extends' keyword to constrain the type parameter to an interface or type with a 'length' property.
steps.expectedOutcome: A generic function 'getLength' that uses a type constraint to ensure the input has a 'length' property.
successCriteria: The 'getLength' function is defined with a constrained type parameter and returns the length of the input value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function uses the 'extends' keyword to constrain the type parameter to types with a 'length' property.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a function named 'getLength' that takes a generic parameter constrained to types with a 'length' property and returns that length.

steps.title: Test constrained generic function with valid and invalid types
steps.instruction: Test your getLength function by calling it with a string (valid) and a number (invalid) to see how TypeScript enforces the constraint.
steps.hint: Call getLength with a string argument, then try calling it with a number argument. TypeScript should allow the first but show an error for the second.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll see that getLength('hello') works correctly, while getLength(42) causes a TypeScript error because numbers don't have a length property.
successCriteria: The getLength function is called with both a string (valid) and a number (invalid), demonstrating how TypeScript enforces the constraint.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to test both cases: call getLength with a string argument and also try calling it with a number argument to see the TypeScript error.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on testing the getLength function. You need to call it with arguments that demonstrate how the constraint works - one that satisfies the constraint (like a string) and one that violates it (like a number).

steps.title: Review and summarize generic type inference concepts
steps.instruction: Add a comment above each generic function you've created (identity, pair, getLength) that explains how TypeScript infers types when calling it.
steps.hint: Write a brief comment describing type inference for each function. For identity, mention that TypeScript can infer T from the argument value. For pair, note that both type parameters can be inferred from the two arguments. For getLength, explain that TypeScript checks the constraint and infers the specific type.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have added explanatory comments that demonstrate your understanding of how TypeScript's type inference works with generics.
successCriteria: Each generic function (identity, pair, getLength) has a comment explaining type inference for that function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some comments, but make sure all three functions (identity, pair, getLength) have explanations about type inference.
steps.feedbackWrong: The code doesn't include the requested comments explaining type inference for each generic function. Try adding brief comments above identity, pair, and getLength.
